lessons.title: Margin Stability and the Pricing Power Test

body.text: Any company can hold its margin in a good year. Pricing power is what you see in the bad one: costs spike, and the margin barely moves.

children.text: Chapter 2 argued that pricing power is the only real test of a brand. This lesson turns that into a measurement you can run on Screener.in in fifteen minutes, and shows you the two traps that make ordinary businesses look like they have pricing power when they do not.
Which Margin to Watch

body.caption: Three margins and what each one tells you

cells: Sales minus raw material and purchased goods cost, divided by sales. On Screener.in, expand the expenses lines in the Profit & Loss to find material cost
The cleanest read on pricing versus input costs
Shown directly in the Profit & Loss section on Screener.in
Pricing power plus cost control and operating leverage together
Distorted by interest, tax, and one-offs, so it is the least useful for this test

body.text: Start with gross margin when you can. Operating margin mixes pricing power with cost cutting, employee costs, and advertising decisions. Gross margin isolates the one question that matters here: did the company keep the gap between what it charges and what its inputs cost?

children.text: Test 1: How Tight Is the Range?
Plot ten years of margin and look at the spread between the best and worst year. A narrow band through boom, crash, and inflation is the signature of a business that sets its own prices.

body.title: Illustrative: Operating Margin Over a Decade (%)

children.text: Both companies average exactly the same margin over the decade: 21.0%. That is where most screeners stop. But A never fell below 19%, while B swung between 10% and 38%. A sets prices. B accepts whatever the market gives it, which is why its worst years leave almost nothing once fixed costs are paid.

body.title: A rough rule for reading the range

children.text: Range under 5 percentage points over a decade: strong evidence of pricing power, common in branded consumer, specialty pharma, and some software businesses.
Range of 5 to 10 points: moderate. Check whether the swings line up with input costs or with demand.
Range above 10 points: the business is largely a price taker. Its margin is set by commodity prices or industry supply, not by the company.
Compare within an industry, never across industries. A 4-point range means something quite different for a cement maker than for a soap maker.
Test 2: What Happened in the Inflation Shock?

FY22 and FY23 gave Indian investors a natural experiment. Crude, palm oil, packaging, and freight costs all rose sharply. Pull up any consumer or industrial company and look at those two years specifically.
Strong pricing power:
gross margin dips for one or two quarters, then returns to its old level as price increases flow through.
Weak pricing power:
gross margin falls and stays down, or the company protects margin by cutting advertising and quality instead of raising prices.
No pricing power:
margin collapses and recovers only when input costs fall again, which tells you the market, not the company, decides.

body.label: The recovery test
body.value: How many quarters did it take for gross margin to return to its pre-shock level?
body.context: Two to four quarters suggests real pricing power. Never recovering, or recovering only once input costs fell, suggests none.

children.text: Test 3: Price Increases With Volume Intact

Raising prices is easy. Raising prices without losing customers is the moat. Most listed consumer companies split their growth into volume and price in their results presentations. The relationship is multiplicative, not additive.

body.caption: Price growth is also called realisation growth

body.title: Split the Growth
body.prompt: A consumer company reports that realisations (prices) rose 6% and volumes rose 5% during the year. What was its value growth, in percent?
body.explanation: Value growth = (1.06 × 1.05) − 1 = 11.3%, not 11%. Adding the two is a close approximation at small numbers but drifts as they grow. Price growth of 6% alongside positive volume growth is the combination that signals genuine pricing power.

body.text: Watch for value growth that is entirely price. If realisations rise 9% while volumes fall 4%, the company is protecting revenue by pushing prices onto a shrinking customer base. That is the pattern that precedes market share loss, not the pattern of a moat.

children.text: Trap 1: Cost Pass-Through Is Not Pricing Power

Many B2B suppliers, including auto component makers and some chemical companies, have contracts that automatically adjust selling prices when raw material prices change. Margins look wonderfully stable. But the customer, not the company, holds the power, and the arrangement protects rupees rather than percentages.

body.caption: A formula-linked contract through a 10% input cost rise (per unit)

children.text: The rupee margin is unchanged at ₹40, but the percentage margin slips from 40.0% to 37.7% because the same profit now sits on a larger revenue base. More importantly, when input costs fall, the price falls too and the company keeps nothing extra. A business with real pricing power keeps some of that benefit.

columns.label: Genuine pricing power
points: The company decides when and how much to raise prices
Margin expands when input costs fall
Price increases stick even after costs normalise
Usually sits with brands, patents, or switching costs
Gross margin trends gently upward over a decade

columns.label: Cost pass-through
points: Contracts or formulas set the price change
Margin percentage falls slightly when costs rise
Prices come back down when input costs fall
Common in auto components and industrial supply
Rupee margin per unit stays flat for years

children.text: Trap 2: Margin Gains That Are Not From Price
A rising operating margin feels like pricing power, but four different forces can produce it. Separate them before drawing conclusions.
Price:
higher realisations per unit. This is pricing power.
Mix:
selling more premium products, as with jewellery moving towards studded pieces or paints towards premium emulsions. Valuable, but it reflects portfolio choices, not power over a given customer.
Cost:
cheaper inputs or better procurement. This reverses when commodity prices turn.
Operating leverage:
fixed costs spread over higher volumes. This reverses in a downturn.

body.title: Diagnose the Margin Move
body.question: A paint company's operating margin rose from 16% to 21% over two years. Crude-linked input costs fell sharply in the same period, volumes grew 4% a year, and management said prices were cut twice to pass on lower costs. What is the most accurate reading?
options: Margin expansion driven mainly by falling input costs, with prices actually being reduced, so this is not evidence of pricing power
Proof the company has an efficient scale moat
body.explanation: Margins rose because inputs got cheaper faster than the company cut prices. The real pricing power test comes on the way back up, when costs rise again. If it can restore prices without losing volumes, the moat is real.

children.text: Test 4: Compare Against the Peer Group

Margin stability means little in isolation. The useful comparison is against two or three listed competitors in the same industry, through the same years. If every player's margin fell 6 points in FY22 and one fell only 1 point, that company has something the others do not.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: A contract that automatically raises the selling price when raw material costs rise protects the company's rupee margin, but it is ___ pass-through, not pricing power.
body.explanation: The customer agreed to a formula, not to the company's pricing decisions. When input costs fall, the price falls with them and no extra margin is retained.

body.title: Two Chemical Companies
body.scenario: You compare two listed specialty chemical companies over ten years. Company P has gross margins between 44% and 47% every year, sells branded formulations to thousands of small customers, and raised prices in FY22 while volumes grew 6%. Company Q has gross margins between 28% and 31%, sells three products to four large multinational customers under formula-linked contracts, and its FY22 presentation notes that price revisions were passed through with a one-quarter lag.
body.prompt: Both look margin-stable. Which one has pricing power, and what would you check to confirm?
body.modelAnswer: Company P has pricing power. It raised prices in an inflationary year and still grew volumes 6%, which means customers accepted the increase. Its customer base is fragmented, so no single buyer can dictate terms, and the margin band is both high and narrow. Company Q's stability is manufactured by contract, not earned. Four customers, three products, and a formula-linked price mean the customers hold the power, and the one-quarter lag confirms prices move because a formula says so. To confirm: for P, check whether gross margin expanded when input costs fell in later years, which would show it kept part of the benefit, and compare its price increases with peers. For Q, check customer concentration in the annual report, whether rupee gross profit per unit has grown at all over a decade, and what happened to its margin when raw material prices declined. Q may still be a decent business with switching costs from being designed into customer processes, but it should not be valued as a company with pricing power.

body.title: Run the Pricing Power Test
steps: Pick a company and two listed peers in the same industry
On Screener.in, note OPM % for the last 10 years for all three, and material cost as a percentage of sales where available
Calculate the range (highest minus lowest) for each company and compare
Look specifically at FY22 and FY23 and count the quarters each took to recover its pre-shock margin
Find the volume and price split in the latest two results presentations
Check the annual report for formula-linked pricing clauses or heavy customer concentration
Conclude: pricing power, cost pass-through, or price taker

body.text: Companies A, B, P, and Q are hypothetical, and the paint example uses illustrative figures. Nothing here is an investment recommendation. Screener.in layouts and disclosure formats may change.

points: Gross margin is the cleanest pricing power signal because it isolates prices against input costs
A narrow margin range across a decade, especially through the FY22 and FY23 inflation, points to pricing power
Value growth = (1 + price growth) × (1 + volume growth) − 1, and price increases alongside steady volumes are the real test
Formula-linked cost pass-through keeps rupee margins stable but is not pricing power, because the company keeps nothing when costs fall
Margin gains can come from price, mix, cheaper inputs, or operating leverage, and only the first is pricing power
Always compare margin behaviour against listed peers through the same years
